The Democratic National Committee's Rules and Bylaws Committee on Friday voted to make the state the first primary contest in 2028, elevating a place with a large Black electorate and sidelining some of the party's longtime early states, Politico reports. Nevada Democrats won’t get to vote first in their party’s ‘28 presidential primary
A bid by Nevada Democrats to vote first in their party’s 2028 presidential primary fell short Friday when a committee recommended that South Carolina repeat as the first-in-the-nation state instead.
A subcommittee of the Democratic National Committee that sets the party’s election calendar made the selection through a vote. South Carolina received 26 votes, Nevada 19 and New Hampshire four.
The entire DNC needs to affirm its Rules and Bylaws Committee’s picks at its next meeting in August. Nevada Democrats are slated to vote first in the West.
Nevada’s effort to vote first in the nation was led by the Nevada State Democratic Party.
“We’ve been consistent all along, putting Nevada first best sets our party up for success,” party Chair Daniele Monroe-Moreno said in a release. “Nevada is the broad coalition of diverse voices — Latino, Black, AANHPI (Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander), and Native American as well as white working-class voters — our party must win back if we’re serious about flipping the White House in 2028.”
Monroe-Moreno said that Nevada will be an early true test for candidates’ ability to win in the general election.
Under the proposed calendar, South Carolina would vote on Jan. 22, 2028.
Nevada Democrats will follow on Feb. 1 and New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia will vote on subsequent Tuesdays until Super Tuesday, which is scheduled for March 7.
“This has never been about one state or one community,” Rep. Steven Horsford, D-Nev., wrote on X. “It’s about building the coalition that wins 270 electoral votes.”
He added: “Nevada is where candidates demonstrate they can unite the diverse coalition Democrats need to win — not just a primary, but the presidency.”
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.
The Associated Press contributed to this story.

South Carolina is on course to remain the lead-off primary in the Democratic Party's 2028 presidential nominating calendar, after landing a key party committee's recommendation.
The Democratic National Committee's (DNC) powerful Rules and Bylaws panel, meeting in the nation's capital on Friday, picked South Carolina over Nevada to hold the party's first presidential nominating contest in 2028, a move that will likely maintain a key role in the primary calendar for Black voters, who are a crucial part of the Democrats' base.
The vote comes after intense lobbying by both states, as well as by New Hampshire, and Iowa over the past year to hold the much-coveted lead-off Democratic primary in the race for the White House. And the battle between South Carolina and Nevada was seen as a struggle between rewarding Black voters, who have long been loyal Democratic voters, and outreach to Latino voters, with whom President Donald Trump and Republicans made major gains in the 2024 election, handing Democrats major setbacks.
The panel also voted to allow Nevada, New Hampshire, Michigan, Virginia, and New Mexico to hold primaries in the early voting window, before the rest of the states hold nominating contests starting ahead of Super Tuesday.

sources.news_title: Democrats Pick South Carolina to Open the 2028 Presidential Primary
sources.text:
A Democratic National Committee (DNC) panel voted on Friday to have South Carolina open the party’s 2028 presidential nominating calendar. South Carolina received 26 votes, Nevada received 19, and New Hampshire received four.
All 49 members of the DNC Rules and Bylaws Committee voted, and 25 votes were required for a majority, according to the committee’s parliamentarian.
The decision is not yet final—the full DNC is scheduled to ratify the calendar at its August meeting.
Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), a member of the committee, said during the meeting that Michigan had asked not to be considered for the lead-off position.
Iowa, which asked the committee in May to lead off the calendar again, lost its region to Michigan. Iowa’s Democratic caucuses had opened the party’s presidential nominating calendar since 1972, until the DNC moved South Carolina to the front for 2024.
In December 2022, President Joe Biden proposed that change and it was accepted by the committee. This time the state was selected in a contested vote among three candidates. South Carolina was pivotal to Biden gaining momentum before Super Tuesday and ultimately winning the 2020 primaries, after facing defeat in Iowa and New Hampshire then coming out ahead in South Carolina.
The committee also voted to expand the early window from five states to six. A resolution the committee adopted in October 2025 had capped the early window at five states and required at least one from each of the party’s four geographic regions.
The committee later in the meeting filled the two remaining slots, completing a six-state early window. In the order approved, South Carolina is projected to vote Jan. 22, 2028, followed by Nevada on Feb. 1, New Hampshire on Feb. 8, New Mexico on Feb. 15, Michigan on Feb. 22, and Virginia on Feb. 29, according to a DNC press release.
In a statement, committee co-chairs Minyon Moore and James Roosevelt Jr. called it the most diverse calendar Democrats have had for an open nominating contest.
The order drew debate. Some members argued that a state from each of the party’s four regions should vote before the two added states—which they said would make the calendar more balanced—noting that New Mexico, added fifth, is scheduled ahead of Michigan, the Midwest’s sole early-window state. A motion to require that failed on a tie vote.
Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) said Michigan’s primary is set by state law for Feb. 22 and the state could not move it, in part because waiver states must confirm by mid-September that they can hold their contest on the assigned date and Michigan’s Republican-led House may not agree to an earlier one.
Democrats began overhauling the calendar after the 2020 Iowa caucuses, when a failure in the state party’s reporting system left the results unresolved for days—something brought up by members at Friday’s meeting.
New Hampshire held its 2024 primary outside the DNC-approved order. State law directs the secretary of state to schedule the primary at least seven days ahead of any similar contest.
Last month the committee amended 2028 delegate selection rules to strengthen penalties for unsanctioned contests.
States that hold one lose all their delegates, including automatic delegates, up from 50 percent, and face a $270,000 fine. Candidates who violate the rules would be barred from DNC debates and from earning delegates in any early-window contest, and campaigns are required to denounce efforts to campaign on their behalf in unsanctioned contests.

Democrats select South Carolina for first presidential nominating contest in '28
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — South Carolina was selected Friday to once again lead off the Democratic Party's 2028 presidential nominating schedule, most likely cementing a dramatic break from decades of tradition by keeping Iowa off the top of the calendar and elevating more racially diverse states.
The decision by the Democratic National Committee's Rules and Bylaws Committee will need to be approved by the full organization, which is scheduled to meet in August.
South Carolina or Nevada had been expected to go first, with each state aggressively campaigning for the coveted spot.
President Joe Biden successfully pushed to move South Carolina to the front of Democrats' 2024 calendar after the state revived his struggling 2020 presidential campaign. South Carolina has long been the first Southern contest and has served as a key test of candidates' support among Black voters.
Jaime Harrison, a former DNC chair in attendance Friday, told The Associated Press after the vote that keeping his home state first on Democrats' nominating calendar signaled to Black voters the value they bring to the party, especially after a Supreme Court decision aimed at weakening their voting power.
"I think we needed a strong statement to say to the most loyal members of our party, which are Black voters, that we're going to stand up with you," said Harrison, who also chaired South Carolina's Democratic Party. "It was just really important for us to stand up and say, 'We see you, we hear you, but most importantly, we're gonna fight like hell for you. And your voices are important.'"
Democratic leaders in a handful of southern states had lobbied for South Carolina to reprise its role as the party's first-in-the-nation contest holder, arguing in a letter to the DNC that the state best represents the initial playing field for presidential candidates to build the coalitions needed to win and serves as "a moral and political compass for our party and our nation."
The overhaul reflects Democrats' effort to give greater influence to states that better mirror the party's diverse coalition, particularly Black and Latino voters, after years of a calendar led by Iowa and New Hampshire, two states with overwhelmingly white electorates.
Much of Friday's debate stood as a contrast on several fronts. South Carolina proponents argued they had the experience to stand up a lead-off primary, and served as a showcase for the Black voters whose support has become vital for Democrats.
"Black voters didn't just show up for this party in 2020. They saved us," Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb said, in making her argument for South Carolina. "They saved our entire country from Donald Trump."
Nevada's supporters, meanwhile, portrayed their state as the party's future, in which they argued Latino voters play a larger and larger role.
"We are the battleground state," said Artie Blanco of Nevada, a DNC vice chair. "We win elections because we leave no voter untouched."
The decision will also shape the opening stage of what is expected to be a crowded Democratic presidential primary. Without an incumbent or clear front-runner, the states that vote first could once again play an outsized role in determining which candidates gain momentum, attract donors and emerge as viable contenders.
Republicans still need to do their calendar. They're expected to stick with their traditional early-state lineup led off by Iowa and New Hampshire.
The calendar decision is one of the first milestones in what's expected to be a tumultuous two-year sprint to the Democratic nomination.
There has not been a truly open Democratic presidential primary — without an incumbent president or a dominant front-runner — in almost two decades.

South Carolina on cusp of being first 2028 Democratic presidential primary state
South Carolina is one step away from becoming the first-in-the-nation Democratic presidential primary state for 2028, after the Democratic National Committee's Rules and Bylaws Committee voted to recommend it at a meeting Friday.
The proposed calendar will be voted on by the full DNC at its summer meeting next month in Austin, Texas.
The other top contender was Nevada, and the panel grappled with whether the party should prioritize its most consistent voting bloc or the fastest-growing demographic group in the country.
In its presentation before the bylaws committee in May, South Carolina representatives argued that it should remain the first primary state in light of the Supreme Court decision on the Voting Rights Act and its impact on Black representation in the South. The Palmetto State also held the first Democratic presidential primary in 2024.
South Carolina advocates have said that removing its status as the first primary contest now would be a "slap in the face" to the Democratic Party's Black voter base.
"This decision is bigger than South Carolina. It's about whether the Democratic Party will stand with the voters who have stood with the party through everything," South Carolina Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain said in May. "Will Democrats meet this moment by supporting the communities on the front lines of defending democracy, or will the Democratic Party tell their most faithful voters they no longer deserve to lead the primary process?"
Advocates for Nevada argued it should be first to weigh in on the presidential nominee because it most closely represents a coalition Democrats need to win nationally. Nevada, they said, includes groups whose support for Democrats has been eroding, like working-class voters, Latinos, Asian American Pacific Islanders, men and low-propensity voters.
Nevada Democratic Party Chair Daniele Monroe-Moreno echoed this sentiment Friday during the debate over the proposed calendar order.
"Nonpartisan voter registration is the largest voter registration block in America now. Why? Because people are mad at both sides of the aisle," Monroe-Moreno said.
And as Democrats consider their nomination calendar, she told the committee, "My state, the state of Nevada, is that coalition that we need to win back."

sources.news_title: Democrats pick South Carolina to open 2028 nomination race, elevating Black voters
sources.text:
By Tim Reid
WASHINGTON, July 24 (Reuters) – South Carolina is poised to remain the Democrats’ first presidential primary state over Nevada after a vote by a powerful party committee on Friday, a racially fraught decision that pitted Black and Latino state leaders against each other.
After two days of sometimes acrimonious debate, the Democratic National Committee’s Rules & Bylaws Committee backed the bid by South Carolina – which has a large Black voter base – to remain the first state to vote on the party’s choice for its 2028 White House nominee. Nevada, which has a significant Latino electorate, had pushed for the top spot.
The DNC is likely to approve Friday’s decision at a full party meeting in August. The initial vote on Friday was close, with South Carolina receiving 26 votes to Nevada’s 19.
The decision is consequential because the first state to vote in a presidential nominating contest often helps to shape the field of candidates, drawing campaign spending and media attention.
During debate, the chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party, Christale Spain, who is Black, said it was crucial for Democrats to make America’s South and its Black voters the start of its nominating process.
Black voters have faced setbacks in battles over political representation this year after a U.S. Supreme court decision hollowed out civil rights legislation, and state legislatures in the South redrew maps that voting rights groups say diluted Black voter power.
“When we are serious about changing this country, Democrats have to start winning in the South,” she said.
Senior Democrats from Nevada sent a letter to the DNC making their case, saying, “Nevada is a small, affordable, competitive battleground where candidates must build the broad, multiracial, working-class coalition that Democrats need to win nationally.”
The competition between the two states became a proxy battle between the party’s Black and Latino bases that exposed early internal divisions ahead of the battle to decide who will become the party’s 2028 White House standard bearer.
South Carolina’s pitch to go first centered on its large Black electorate, a crucial national voting bloc for Democrats that President Donald Trump and Republicans have drawn voters from in recent years.
Nevada countered that unlike Republican-led South Carolina, it is a key presidential battleground state with a large Hispanic population and a strong blue-collar union presence, two constituencies that Democrats must work harder to +win over in future elections.
In 2022, former Democratic President Joe Biden persuaded Democrats to overhaul their 2024 nominating calendar, ending Iowa’s first-in-the-nation status and putting South Carolina first. Nevada was put in second place.
Friday’s vote by the powerful DNC committee reflected robust pitches by South Carolina and Nevada in the fight for first place and late-night lobbying by party leaders on Thursday.
(Reporting by Tim Reid in Washington, editing by Ross Colvin and Alistair Bell)

sources.text:
South Carolina is poised to hold the first Democratic presidential nominating contest in 2028 after the Democratic National Committee’s powerful rules committee voted to keep the state at the front of the line.
The move, recommended by the rules committee Friday and set to be presented to the full DNC at its summer meeting next month, settles a monthslong battle among a handful of states.
Nevada and New Hampshire, which also vied to be the lead-off state, will hold the second and third nominating contests, respectively. New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia will round out the first six contests prior to Super Tuesday.
The move officially pushes Iowa out of the early voting window altogether. It had served as the opening contest for both parties up until 2024, when Democrats pushed it back after issues with the 2020 caucuses.
The new calendar significantly changes the calculus for Democratic presidential candidates, replacing two heavily white states at the top with states with more diverse populations, while still preserving three of the four traditional early state contests. And adding two more states before Super Tuesday means there will be more delegates up for grabs for candidates to win before March.
The race to kick off the Democrats’ presidential nominating contest was hard-fought and drawn-out, with states first pitching DNC rules committee members during a January meeting in Puerto Rico and continuing to press hard in the months since.
The struggle between Nevada and South Carolina turned tense in recent weeks, particularly among some who framed the debate as one between two key pieces of the Democratic Party’s base. Latino voters make up a large portion of the Nevada electorate, and Black voters are the foundation of South Carolina’s Democratic electorate.
Key Democrats from both states leaned heavily on DNC members and sought to sway broader public opinion in the party.
“When South Carolina goes first … the Deep South goes first, Black voters go first,” South Carolina Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain said this week during an interview with political commentator Roland Martin. “Black voters are the backbone of this party, and so we should continue to elevate Black voters’ role in the process, not push it further back.”
Nevada put on the hard sell too, with a host of lawmakers, Latino groups and influential labor leaders mounting an aggressive lobbying effort. They highlighted the importance of winning over voters in a critical battleground state as Democrats look to rebound from the 2024 election, when President Donald Trump won Nevada.
“Democrats keep losing working-class voters because we keep skipping the states where they actually live. To win Nevada, you have to earn Latino voters, Black voters, AANHPI voters, AND white working-class voters — all at once,” Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, the Democratic nominee for governor, wrote on the social media platform X this week.
South Carolina Democrats’ effort got a jolt of momentum in the wake of the Supreme Court’s decision to weaken part of the Voting Rights Act, a move that prompted a number of Republican-controlled states to redraw majority-minority districts represented largely by Black Democrats.
The Palmetto State’s supporters repeatedly referenced the Supreme Court decision and the struggle for Black voters in the South to gain voting rights during the Civil Rights Movement.
Donna Brazile, a rules committee member and former national party chair, emotionally evoked Barbara Jordan, a Black Democratic political icon, and criticized the Supreme Court’s ruling.
“If we believe in the future, the future that Barbara Jordan called us to build,” Brazile said, “we must begin the 2028 presidential primary season in the South.”
Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, backing South Carolina, told members that “we need to send a message that we are not abandoning people that have been part of this party, and are being screwed by the Supreme Court,” even as she pushed back on the idea that the vote would elevate South Carolina over the other states in the early window.
“There are going to be six states that are first in the country to make sure that every single segment of the Democratic Party, and those we need to bring back, are going to be part of this story,” she said.
The decision marks the latest step in a significant reshuffling of past competitive Democratic presidential contests, with Iowa and New Hampshire long holding the first two contests.
But a botched 2020 Iowa caucus — in which a series of technological failures delayed the results — and a movement among some Democrats to elevate more racially diverse states prompted change in 2024.
Then-President Joe Biden pushed the DNC to reshuffle the primary calendar for his re-election year, moving South Carolina to the front of the line four years after it provided the key result for his 2020 primary campaign. The DNC also gave Georgia and Michigan the right to hold their contests during the pivotal early window. Michigan followed through, while Republican lawmakers in Georgia declined to bless the plan.
New Hampshire sought to disregard the DNC and hold its Democratic primary in January, with the party initially punishing the state but ultimately relenting, as it regularly has whenever states flout its calendar.
New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Ray Buckley criticized the DNC’s decision, noting that state law requires them to hold the first presidential primary.
“Today’s vote shows that many party insiders have learned nothing from 2024,” Buckley said in a statement. “New Hampshire has a proven track record of testing our candidates with a rigorous, fair, and efficient process, yet those qualities did not prevail. This committee’s vote does not change the realities governing New Hampshire’s primary, which are beyond the control of both this committee and our state party.”
The New Hampshire Democratic Party did not immediately respond to a question as to whether it would follow the national party’s wishes or once again hold a rogue contest.
Asked about whether New Hampshire would follow the new rules, DNC Chairman Ken Martin praised Buckley as a “mentor” and the state for its “very proud tradition of civic participation, engagement in their primary.”
“My hope is that New Hampshire is still represented in this process,” Martin said, adding that if there are any concerns in the coming months, “we’ll have to cross that bridge when we get there.”
After South Carolina holds its primary on Jan. 22, Nevada will follow on Feb. 1 and New Hampshire on Feb. 8. Then, candidates will head to New Mexico for the Feb. 15 contest, to Michigan on Feb. 22 and Virginia on Feb. 29.
On top of changes to the 2028 calendar, the DNC is expected to adopt stronger punishments for states that choose to flout the party’s approved calendar.
Those new punishments would include stripping these states of all delegates, fining the state party $270,000, banning candidates from official party debates if they campaign in unsanctioned contests — and making it harder for the party to backtrack on or wipe out these penalties later, if a state like New Hampshire does decide to flout the rules and hold an unsanctioned primary.
Winning the national party’s blessing to hold a nominating contest ahead of Super Tuesday is a big prize for state Democratic Party organizations, given how these early contests have helped to shape the path of modern presidential nominations.
Biden’s 2020 campaign may not have ever taken off if not for a big win in South Carolina, where he leaned on his strong relationships with Black voters for a commanding victory after sputtering in Iowa and New Hampshire. Four years prior, Sen. Bernie Sanders’ strong showings in those first two contests sent a powerful signal to a Democratic establishment that had hoped former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton would cruise to the nomination.
While a dozen states made the pitch to DNC rules committee members over the last few months, some always faced significant practical concerns. States like North Carolina, Tennessee and Georgia pitched themselves for early contests, but Democrats would have needed Republican support in the state legislatures to change primary dates.
Meanwhile, Republicans are not expected to make substantial changes to their calendar ahead of an open 2028 presidential contest of their own.

The decision by the Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee will need to be approved by the full organization, which is scheduled to meet in August.
South Carolina or Nevada had been expected to go first, with each state aggressively campaigning for the coveted spot.

sources.text:
Topline
The first Democratic primaries in the next presidential election are likely to be held in South Carolina, the Democratic National Committee signed Friday, pushing Nevada and New Hampshire primaries to later in the season and giving southern Black voters the chance to shape the race from the outset.
Key Facts
The decision by the DNC’s rules committee still needs to be approved by the full body later this summer but, on Friday, South Carolina was informally selected as the leader of the 2028 primary season for the Democrats.
South Carolina held the first Democratic presidential primary in 2024, as well, which marked the first time in decades Iowa and New Hampshire were snubbed in opening the party’s nominating process.
Moving South Carolina to the front of the line is a result of the party's push to elevate the electorate of a more diverse state and will allow candidates to appeal to Black voters—which make up a large part of South Carolina's Democratic primary electorate—before competing elsewhere.
South Carolina was in tough competition with Nevada, a swing state where a large contingency of Latinos cast their vote, for the first primary, but committee members argued that Black Democrats are the party's most loyal voting bloc and ultimately chose the southern state.
In addition to South Carolina, the DNC rules committee chose Nevada, New Hampshire, Michigan, New Mexico and Virginia as the six states to host primaries before Super Tuesday.
This is the first time New Mexico and Virginia have been added to the early window.
CRUCIAL QUOTE
“When South Carolina goes first… the Deep South goes first, Black voters go first,” South Carolina Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain said earlier this week. “Black voters are the backbone of this party, and so we should continue to elevate Black voters’ role in the process, not push it further back.”
BIG NUMBER
76.5%. That's the percentage of South Carolina's early voters in the 2024 Democratic primary who were Black. Roughly 25% of South Carolina residents are Black and, historically, Black voters have made up more than half of South Carolina Democratic primary voters.
what to watch for
Which states the Republicans choose. The Republican National Committee has not announced its official 2028 presidential nominating calendar yet, but party leaders are widely expected to keep the traditional early-state lineup of Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina and Nevada.
Key background
The order in which states vote in the presidential primary process is important for fundraising, media attention and political momentum that can often shape the rest of the race and can quickly elevate—or sink—a campaign. In the case of the Democrats, a first primary in South Carolina could give an advantage to candidates with strong ties to southern or Black voters. Both parties choose their early voting states based on what electorates they believe will test their candidates in a way that reflects the broader nation and predicts how its priorities will play with various demographics. Democrats say their early-state lineup is designed to test presidential candidates with a racially and geographically diverse coalition—including Black, Latino, union and Midwestern voters—that they think will reflect the voters needed to win a general election. Republicans have said the traditional sequence, starting with Iowa, gives lesser-known candidates a chance to build support through on-the-ground campaigning and face-to-face voter engagement before larger states vote.

Democrats select South Carolina to kick off presidential nominating contest in 2028, leave Iowa out
WASHINGTON (AP) — South Carolina was selected Friday to once again lead off the Democratic Party’s 2028 presidential nominating schedule, cementing a dramatic break from decades of tradition by leaving Iowa out of the early-state lineup altogether and elevating more racially diverse states.
The decision by the Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee will need to be approved by the full organization, which is scheduled to meet in August.
Nevada is expected to follow South Carolina, with New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia rounding out the early-state calendar. Those states will wield outsized influence in the nominating contest before Super Tuesday, when voters across a large group of states cast presidential primary ballots.
“This calendar will battle test our candidates, ensure our nominee can appeal to broad swaths of the electorate and this calendar will allow voters, not money, but voters to be the ultimate decider,” DNC Chair Ken Martin said after the vote.
The overhaul reflects Democrats’ effort to give greater influence to states that better mirror the party’s diverse coalition, particularly Black and Latino voters, after years of a calendar led by Iowa and New Hampshire, two states with overwhelmingly white electorates.
But hopes of emerging from Friday’s meeting with a party unified around one map were dashed by anger from states that had previously led the process. Rita Hart, chair of the Iowa Democratic Party, said she was disappointed but not surprised by Friday’s calendar vote, which she called “very messy” and a sign that the national party is “out of touch with voters.”
There was more angst in New Hampshire, where the secretary of state is required by law to schedule its presidential primary at least seven days before any other state holds a similar contest, setting up a potential conflict with the DNC calendar.
“The Democratic National Committee’s decision today is wrong for Democrats, wrong for New Hampshire, and wrong for the country,” said a group of congressional leaders in New Hampshire, including Sens. Jeanne Shaheen and Maggie Hassan.
Democrats elevate more diverse states
Democrats opted to lead with South Carolina after President Joe Biden successfully pushed to move the state to the front of Democrats’ 2024 calendar after the state revived his struggling 2020 presidential campaign. South Carolina has long been the first Southern contest and has served as a key test of candidates’ support among Black voters.
Jaime Harrison, a former DNC chair in attendance Friday, told The Associated Press after the vote that keeping his home state first on Democrats’ nominating calendar signaled to Black voters the value they bring to the party, especially after a Supreme Court decision aimed at weakening their voting power.
“I think we needed a strong statement to say to the most loyal members of our party, which are Black voters, that we’re going to stand up with you,” said Harrison, who also chaired South Carolina’s Democratic Party. “It was just really important for us to stand up and say, ’We see you, we hear you, but most importantly, we’re gonna fight like hell for you. And your voices are important.’”
Much of Friday’s debate stood as a contrast on several fronts. South Carolina proponents argued they had the experience to stand up a lead-off primary, and served as a showcase for the Black voters whose support has become vital for Democrats.
“Black voters didn’t just show up for this party in 2020. They saved us,” Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb said, in making her argument for South Carolina. “They saved our entire country from Donald Trump.”
Nevada’s supporters, meanwhile, portrayed their state as the party’s future, in which they argued Latino voters play a larger and larger role.
“We are the battleground state,” said Artie Blanco of Nevada, a DNC vice chair. “We win elections because we leave no voter untouched.”
Republicans still need to do their calendar. They’re expected to stick with their traditional early-state lineup led off by Iowa and New Hampshire.
Anger emerges from states that are not selected
Iowa has long led both parties’ calendars with caucuses. Hart declined to say whether Iowa Democrats will defy the national party in 2028. She said they will wait until after the state’s midterm races when Democrats hope to make recently unattainable gains in the increasingly conservative state.
“We’re going to win elections here, and then we’re going to tell them what we’re going to do,” said Scott Brennan, who formerly represented Iowa on the DNC’s Rules and Bylaws Committee.
New Hampshire Democrats similarly would not commit Friday to following the new calendar.
“This committee’s vote does not change the realities governing New Hampshire’s primary, which are beyond the control of both this committee and our state party,” said New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Ray Buckley.
Asked about some states not committing to the new calendar, Martin said the party will “have to cross that bridge when we get there.”
“We got some time, and the calendar was just set here,” said Martin.
The new map will shape the opening stage of what is expected to be a crowded Democratic presidential primary. Without an incumbent or clear front-runner, the states that vote first could once again play an outsized role in determining which candidates gain momentum, attract donors and emerge as viable contenders.
The calendar decision is one of the first milestones in what’s expected to be a tumultuous two-year sprint to the Democratic nomination.
There has not been a truly open Democratic presidential primary — without an incumbent president or a dominant front-runner — in almost two decades.
